passage:
Monday: Harish and Ojas argued over whose turn it was on the carrom board at the society clubhouse. It ended in a sulk.
Tuesday: The argument started again at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching. Ojas said Harish cheated. Harish felt every eye on him, and his chest went tight. "At least I didn't cry on sports day in Class 2 like you," he said, loudly. Someone laughed. "And your dad's scooter sounds like a sick goat." More laughter. Harish didn't care about carrom anymore; he only needed to win.
Friday: Ojas sat at the far end of the bus. Harish kept looking at the back of his head. The laughter from Tuesday didn't feel so good now.

qa.q: Where did the second argument happen, and who was watching?
qa.a: It happened at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching.

qa.q: Why did Harish bring up Ojas's dad and sports day at the bus stop?
qa.a: With every eye on him he felt cornered, so winning mattered more than the carrom game and he picked words meant to hurt.

qa.q: What could have stopped the stakes rising at the bus stop?
qa.a: Harish could have noticed his tight chest and said "Let's sort it later", or an older kid could have split them up before the crowd made it a show.

qa.q: What is it like for Ojas by Friday?
qa.a: Ojas seems hurt and wants distance, sitting at the far end of the bus after being laughed at about his dad in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child, cornered in front of onlookers, dragging in an old embarrassment and mocking a friend's family just to win.

passage: Sit, Vikas. You think your Dadi never fought? When I was nine, Sunaina and I quarrelled over a skipping rope in the lane behind the mill. Other girls gathered round, and that crowd made me feel trapped. I had to win. So I dug up old things: how she had copied my sums in Class 3, how her frocks were always hand-me-downs from her cousins. The girls went "Oooh." Sunaina's face crumpled and she ran home. I stood there with the rope, feeling like a queen for one minute. Then the lane was empty, and the rope was just a rope. It took us a whole summer to talk properly again. That is why I stopped you today, beta, when you started on your friend's mother.

qa.q: What were Dadi and Sunaina quarrelling over?
qa.a: They quarrelled over a skipping rope in the lane behind the mill.

qa.q: How did the crowd of girls make young Dadi feel?
qa.a: The crowd made her feel trapped, so she felt she had to win, even by saying things meant to hurt Sunaina.

qa.q: What could young Dadi have done when she felt trapped by the crowd?
qa.a: She could have said she didn't want to fight in front of everyone and walked away, then talked to Sunaina alone later about the rope.

qa.q: How was Sunaina affected when the old things were brought up?
qa.a: Sunaina was hurt and shamed in front of the other girls; her face crumpled and she ran home, and it took a whole summer to mend.

grounding: Shows a child who, feeling trapped by an audience, digs up old grievances and mocks a friend's clothes and family to win.

passage:
Tuesday: Madhav and Ankita argued over the cricket bat in the school yard. "You hog it," Ankita said. "You bat like a chicken," said Madhav. The bell rang.
Wednesday: The whole class was watching this time. Ankita said, "Remember when you cried in the Class 3 play?" Some of them laughed. Madhav felt trapped. He heard himself say, "At least my teeth don't stick out like yours," and then, "Your whole family is weird." He wanted it to hurt, and it did.
Thursday: Ankita ate lunch in the library. Madhav's stomach felt sick every time he passed the door.

qa.q: What did Ankita bring up on Wednesday in front of the class?
qa.a: She reminded everyone that Madhav cried in the Class 3 play.

qa.q: Why did Madhav say hurtful things about Ankita's teeth and family?
qa.a: He felt cornered and humiliated when the class laughed, so winning mattered more than the bat and he chose words meant to hurt.

qa.q: What turning point could still help after Wednesday?
qa.a: Madhav could admit to Ankita that his words about her teeth and family were unfair, or a teacher could help them talk without the class watching.

qa.q: What might Ankita be experiencing on Thursday?
qa.a: She seems hurt and ashamed, choosing the library so she does not have to face the class or Madhav.

grounding: Over three days a quarrel over a bat escalates: with an audience, a boy drags in old stuff and insults a friend's looks and family to win.

passage:
Sit, sit. You want to know why Rekha and I never fell out again? Because of one day when we were nine.
I am your Alka Nani, but back then I was a sharp-tongued girl with pigtails. Rekha got the good skipping rope first, and in front of all the girls in the lane I brought up the time she stole my ribbon in Class 2. Then I laughed at her mother's torn sari. Everyone went "ooh." I felt like a queen for one second.
Rekha didn't cry. She just picked up her slippers and went home. For a week her door stayed shut to me.
That was the day I learned what my mouth could do.

qa.q: What did Alka Nani bring up in front of the girls in the lane?
qa.a: She brought up the time Rekha stole her ribbon in Class 2, and then laughed at Rekha's mother's torn sari.

qa.q: What was young Alka feeling in the moment she said those things?
qa.a: She felt powerful and triumphant for a second, like a queen, because the audience reacted, though the win was really about not losing face.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Alka have turned things around?
qa.a: When the girls went "ooh," she could have stopped and gone back to the rope, instead of mocking Rekha's mother; that was the moment winning began to matter more than the game.

qa.q: What was Rekha going through when she picked up her slippers and left?
qa.a: She was deeply hurt and humiliated, too wounded to answer back, and she shut her door for a week.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a girl in front of an audience, she dragged up an old grievance and mocked a friend's family to win, and how much it hurt.

passage:
The school bus was stuck behind a fallen tree, rain drumming on the roof, and thirty children had nothing to do but listen.
It had started over a window seat. Now Seema said, "You're just jealous, Irawati."
Irawati felt every head turn toward her. Her face burned. "Jealous? Of you? You copied my science project last year and everyone knows it." A few kids gasped. She kept going. "And your glasses are so thick you probably can't even see the window."
Someone at the back laughed. Irawati didn't care about the seat anymore. She only cared about not losing.
Seema turned to the fogged glass and said nothing at all.

qa.q: Why was the school bus stuck?
qa.a: It was stuck behind a fallen tree in the rain.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when every head turned toward her?
qa.a: She felt cornered and embarrassed, with a burning face, so she reached for old grievances and insults just to avoid losing.

qa.q: What turning point could still change things on the bus?
qa.a: Irawati could stop after the first insult and say "Sorry, that was mean," or the bus attendant could move them apart before it gets more personal.

qa.q: What is Seema experiencing when she turns to the window?
qa.a: She seems hurt and exposed in front of thirty children, so she goes silent rather than fight back.

grounding: Stuck on a bus with an audience, a girl stops caring about the seat and drags in an old grievance and an insult about a friend's looks to win.

passage:
The badminton game in the colony compound had started as fun. Then Rajni called Minakshi's shot "out" and six kids gathered to watch.

"It was IN," said Minakshi. "You always cheat. Like last month in hopscotch."

"That was different!"

Everyone was looking. Minakshi's face burned. She wanted to win this more than she wanted the point. "At least my mother doesn't shout so loud the whole building hears," she said.

Rajni went very quiet. Her racket slipped down to her side.

Someone said "Ooooh." Minakshi felt a quick flash of triumph, and then, right behind it, something cold in her stomach. She had meant it to hurt. She could see that it had.

Rajni turned and walked towards her building without a word.

qa.q: What did Rajni call Minakshi's shot?
qa.a: Rajni called Minakshi's shot "out".

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling right after the insult?
qa.a: She felt a quick flash of triumph followed by a cold, guilty feeling, seeing that her words really hurt Rajni.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do now to stop things getting worse?
qa.a: She could follow Rajni or find her later, say sorry for the words about her mother, and leave the shot argument aside.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni to hear that insult in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rajni is deeply hurt and embarrassed, since something painful about her family was used against her with others watching.

grounding: With an audience watching, a child drags in an old grievance and insults a friend's family, caring more about winning than the game.
